vignette: Elena remembers the cold tile against her back before she remembers anything else. It was three years ago, in a basement she did not recognize, where the questions stopped mattering after the seventh hour. The men who held her did not speak her language well, but their hands translated everything. She learned to go quiet, to fold herself inward until her ribs felt like empty shells. When they finally let her go, stumbling out into a street she could not place, she thought the worst was over. She was wrong. Now, at twenty-seven, Elena wakes before her alarm. Her sheets are tangled around her legs, damp with sweat. She lies still, counting the floorboards in her studio apartment, waiting for the silence to feel safe. It never does. By the time her boots touch the cold floor, her shoulders are already locked. She showers quickly, scrubbing until her skin burns, though no dirt clings to her. On Sundays, her mother calls from another country. Lately, Elena lets it go to voicemail. Spanish feels too soft now. Her work van holds the smell of refrigerant and old dust. As an HVAC technician, she spends her days in attics, crawlspaces, and mechanical rooms, tightening copper lines and diagnosing failing compressors. Now, the work feels like walking through a minefield she cannot see. When she slips into a narrow utility closet to check a furnace, her breath catches. Her gloves feel too thick, then too thin. Her mind supplies the image of zip ties, of breath being counted, of a ratcheting wrench echoing in a place where time had no meaning. She backs out, wipes her hands on her pants, and texts her supervisor she is taking an early lunch. She sits in her truck with the engine off, watching the streetlights flicker on, until her pulse slows enough to climb back down. She has stopped going to places where strangers gather. The grocery store aisles feel like corridors she once walked blindfolded. She orders supplies online and leaves the packages unopened on her porch until evening. Friends from trade school send invitations to weekends in the mountains, to dinners at the community center. She replies with short messages, then puts her phone face-down on the counter. The truth is quieter: she is exhausted from holding herself together. Today, she sits in the chair by the window, her work boots still on, laces pulled tight. Her hands rest on her knees, palms up, a habit from a time when open hands meant survival. She watches a sparrow land on the sill, then jump away at the sound of a passing siren. She does not flinch, but her jaw tightens. When asked how the week was, she looks at her boots. She describes the temperature drop in a commercial building last Tuesday, the way she traced a leak in a duct until her fingers went numb. She speaks in a low, steady voice. But when the clinician mentions the word "corner," she stops. Her gaze drops. Her breathing becomes shallow, measured, controlled. She is not in the room. She is somewhere else, counting, waiting, surviving. The clinician does not rush her. They sit in the quiet until her shoulders drop a fraction of an inch, until she looks up and says the sun feels a little less heavy today.
